overview.description: Sueca (Portuguese: 'Swedish') is the most popular card game in Portugal and Brazil. It is a trick-taking game for 4 players in two partnerships. The game uses a 40-card deck and is notable for its Ace-Seven-King-Jack-Queen hierarchy (similar to Briscola or Tressette, but with 7 as 10 points). The goal is to take more than half the points (61+) in tricks. No talking is allowed.

history.origins: Likely derives from Tressette or similar Italian games, perhaps brought by Swedish sailors?
timeline: 1900s: Massive popularity in Brazil and Angola.
history.evolution: The ranking (A > 7 > K > J > Q) is distinct.
history.cultural: Often played loudly ('Bater a carta') despite the no-talking rule.

setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck with the 8s, 9s and 10s removed, leaving 40 cards. Four suits; rank in each suit from high to low: Ace, 7 (manilha), King, Jack, Queen, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2.
setup.dealing: Deal 10 cards to each player. Bottom card turned for Trump.

rules.objective: Win more than 60 of the 120 card points in tricks; first team to four games wins the rubber.
rules.gameplay: Player to dealer's right leads. Players must follow suit if able; may play any card if void. If any trump is played, highest trump wins the trick; otherwise highest card of the led suit wins. Winner of each trick leads to the next. No signals between partners.
keyRules: Trump suit from turned bottom card of deck.
Highest trump wins trick; if no trumps, highest of led suit.
No signals or communication between partners.
120 points total in deck; need more than 60 to win a game.

strategy.basic: Draw trumps early if you have the Ace or Seven. If partner leads a suit and you have the Ace, play it immediately to secure the points unless the trick is already won. Don't be afraid to trump low if you can win.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Seven' Trap: The King (4 pts) is often sacrificed to save the Seven (10 pts). Don't lead a Seven if the Ace is out.
strategy.advanced: Counting the 120: If opponents have 60, you can't win. If you have 61, stop risking high cards. Play safe.

list.description: In the Azores the 10 is often the manilha (second highest). Trump determined by cutting the packet of 12 rejected cards (9s, 8s, 7s) instead of turning a card.
